title: The Side-by-Side Principle
hook: Men often talk best when they are not facing each other: in the car, on a walk, at the bar, eyes on the same thing instead of on each other.
why:
Ask a man where he had the most honest conversation of his life and the answer is often a place, not a person: a long drive, a fishing trip, a building site at the end of a shift, a bench outside a hospital. What these places share is geometry. The two people were beside each other, looking at the same thing, rather than across a table looking at each other.

Earlier chapters in this book used that geometry for one purpose: asking hard questions. This chapter treats it as a principle of men's friendship in its own right. It sets out what the research says about side-by-side and face-to-face friendship, and how much of the popular picture survives; why sitting or walking beside someone makes talk easier; what you lose when you cannot see a face, and how to read a person anyway; when it is time to turn and face someone; and how to build side-by-side time into a life that has slowly run out of it.

teach.p:
In 1982 the psychologist Paul Wright offered a phrase that has followed men's friendships ever since. Women's friendships, he wrote, tend to be face to face: the friends attend to each other directly, and talk is the main business. Men's friendships tend to be side by side: the friends attend to something else together, a game, a job, a shared interest, and closeness grows out of the doing. In the same year, Mayta Caldwell and Letitia Anne Peplau asked students what they would rather do with a friend, and found that women more often chose just talking, while men more often chose an activity.

The phrase stuck because it described something people recognised. It also tempted a lazy conclusion, that men's friendships are shallower. Wright argued against that from the start, and later urged caution about the differences themselves. When Jeffrey Hall pooled 37 studies of what people expect from a friend in a 2011 meta-analysis, women did expect more self-disclosure and intimacy from friends, and men placed more weight on shared activity and status. But the differences were modest, and the two groups overlapped heavily. Many men want to talk; many women bond by doing.

So treat side by side as a common preference, not a law of nature or a ceiling on what men can share. Its value in this chapter is practical. It describes a setting in which many men find it easier to open up, and a setting you can choose on purpose.

The figures here stand shoulder to shoulder, facing the same way, at ease. Nothing about the position is distant. It simply puts the attention somewhere other than on each other's faces, and for many men that is what makes the rest possible.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men, on average, showed no preference for activity-based friendship. Hall's meta-analysis found a real but modest difference with heavy overlap, so the principle describes a tendency, and any particular man may be the exception.
teach.pullQuote: Side by side is a common preference, not a ceiling on what men can share.

teach.h: Why it works: a face is heavy to hold.
teach.p:
A face is the richest thing in anyone's field of view, and holding eye contact while you think is work. The chapter on gaze described Arthur Glenberg's finding that people look away more when questions get harder, and answer difficult questions more accurately when they are allowed to avert their eyes. Face to face, every hesitation is visible, every glance away can feel like evasion, and both people are monitoring each other while trying to find words.

Side by side removes most of that load. Neither person has to manage their face or watch for the other's reaction second by second. A pause becomes a natural part of looking at the road or the water rather than an awkward gap. Difficult things can be said to the windscreen. If the subject becomes too much, either person can look at the view, comment on it and come back later, without a visible retreat.

There is also less sense of being on the spot. Across a table, a conversation can feel like an interview, especially between men who are not used to talking about personal matters. The arrangement itself announces that this is a serious talk. Beside each other, the setting says the opposite: we are just here, doing this, and talk is a by-product. That lowers the stakes enough for some things to be said that would never be said if they had to be announced.

The figures here face each other squarely. For many conversations this is fine. For a man who finds personal talk difficult, it can feel like a spotlight, and the most useful thing you can do is move the conversation somewhere the spotlight is not.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people disclosed as much, and found it as easy, face to face as side by side. The evidence on gaze and thinking is strong, but direct comparisons of disclosure in the two arrangements are few, so treat this as a well-supported explanation rather than a proven one.

teach.p:
Side by side does more than remove a burden. Looking at the same thing at the same time seems to build something of its own. In 2014 Erica Boothby, Margaret Clark and John Bargh asked people to taste chocolate at the same moment as another participant who was tasting the same chocolate, or while that person did something else. The two people did not speak. When the experience was shared, pleasant chocolate was rated more pleasant and bitter chocolate more unpleasant. Simply attending to the same thing at the same time made the experience stronger.

The idea is old. The chapter on gaze described how infants learn to follow another person's gaze and look at what they are looking at, the joint attention on which much of human learning rests. Adults never lose the pleasure of it. Watching a match together, staring at a fire, looking at an engine with its bonnet up, or standing at the edge of a cliff in the wind are all ways of being in the same experience without having to talk about it.

For friendships between men, this matters. A great deal of what is shared side by side is never put into words: the tension of the last ten minutes of a game, the satisfaction when the job finally works, the quiet at the end of a long walk. It still counts. It is part of what makes two people feel that they have been through something together.

The figures here sit on a bench, looking the same way. One is turned slightly toward the other, but both are mostly attending to what is in front of them. The bench does some of the work of friendship for them.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if sharing an experience without words made no difference to how it felt. Boothby and colleagues found that it did, though their studies were small laboratory tasks, and how far the effect extends to friendship is a reasonable inference rather than a measured result.

teach.p:
Side by side comes in several forms, and each has its own character. A walk sets a shared rhythm and a shared direction. It also seems to loosen thinking: in 2014 Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz found that most of the people in their studies came up with more creative ideas while walking than while sitting. Many people find that a problem which went round in circles at a desk opens up on a path.

A drive has other advantages. Nobody can leave until the destination, eye contact is impossible for the driver and unnecessary for the passenger, and the journey has a natural end that limits how long a hard conversation must last. Parents of teenagers often find that the car is where they hear the most, for exactly these reasons. Its limits are equally clear: the driver's attention belongs to the road, so a conversation that becomes distressing should wait until the car has stopped.

Working together, on a garden, a car, a kitchen or a shared project, gives the hands something to do while the mouth decides what to say. Talk comes in fragments between tasks, and long silences are normal. The chapter on shared activity later in this part looks at this form in depth.

Choose the form to suit the person and the moment. A walk suits someone who needs to move and think. A drive suits someone who needs a contained space and a fixed end. A job suits someone who finds talking for its own sake hard. The figures here walk at the same pace, one glancing across before looking back at the path. Most of the conversation happens in that glance and the steps that follow it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if walking, driving and working side by side made conversation no easier than sitting face to face. The walking result concerned creative thinking rather than personal talk, so its application here is an extrapolation.

teach.p:
The price of side by side is that you lose most of the face. You can glance across, but you cannot watch someone's expression continuously without breaking the arrangement that made them comfortable. So you need to read through other channels, and the earlier chapters have prepared you for this.

Listen to the voice, as the chapter on voice described: changes in pace, pitch and volume, the voice dropping as a subject gets closer to the bone, the pause before a hard word. Listen to the breath, as the chapter on breath described: a long exhale, a held breath, a sigh. Watch the hands in your peripheral vision: still or busy, gripping the wheel, turning a cup, picking at a label. Notice the pace: a walk that slows or stops, a job that is suddenly abandoned, a fishing line left untended.

Notice, above all, when the arrangement changes. When someone who has been looking at the road turns to look at you, they are often checking how you are taking what they have just said, or preparing to say something more important. Meet the glance briefly, nod, and look back at the view if that seems to be what they want. When someone stops walking, the next sentence is usually the one that matters.

Read your own position too. If you keep turning to stare at a man who is trying to talk to the windscreen, you are putting the spotlight back. The figures here stand side by side, one with a hand in a pocket, the other shifting his weight. In this position, a hand coming out of a pocket, a step closer or a turn of the head is a large event, and worth noticing.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if voice, breath, hands and pace carried no information about a person's state when the face was hidden. The earlier chapters on voice and breath show that they do, though less precisely than a confident reader might assume, so check what you think you have heard by asking.

teach.p:
Side by side is not always the right arrangement. Some things need the face. An apology, as the chapter on repair later in this part explains, is weakened if it is delivered to the side of someone's head. A declaration of love, an announcement of bad news, a decision that will change a relationship, all ask for the other person to see you, and to see that you are seeing them.

Some people also prefer face to face, and should not be pushed beside you because it is easier for you. Many women, and many men, feel that a serious conversation conducted while staring at a road is a conversation in which the other person is hiding. Preferences vary between cultures, families and individuals. If someone keeps turning toward you, they may be asking for your full attention.

And side by side can become a way of avoiding. Two men can spend twenty years beside each other at matches without either of them ever saying that something is wrong. The arrangement makes talk easier; it does not make it happen. At some point, someone has to say the thing.

A useful middle position is the one the chapter on proxemics described: seated or standing at an angle, roughly at a corner of a table, so that both people can look at each other or away as they choose. The figures here stand angled toward each other, open but not confronting. Turning from beside someone to face them is itself a signal. Do it when the moment calls for it, and say why: “I want to look at you while I say this.”
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if apologies and serious announcements were received equally well whether or not the speaker faced the listener. The claim rests on research on apology and on common experience rather than on direct tests of seating, so treat it as strong advice, not a law.

teach.p:
The most common problem with side-by-side friendship is not that it fails but that it fades. School, sport, work and neighbourhood once supplied men with regular activities alongside other men. Adult life removes them one by one: teams break up, jobs change, people move, children arrive, and the occasions for standing beside a friend disappear. Many men discover in their forties that they have acquaintances but no one to call, and do not know how to begin again.

Because the activity is the setting for the friendship, the fix is often to restore the activity rather than to schedule a conversation. Invite a friend to do something with you, not to talk: help with a job, a walk, a match, a drive to collect something. Make it regular if you can, because repeated time beside someone builds more than a single long evening. The chapter on shared activity looks at how much time friendship takes.

Use the same principle with the people closest to you. A father and son, two brothers, a man and his ageing father often talk most freely in the car or the garden. If a relationship has gone quiet, try changing where and how you are together before trying to change what you say.

The figures here sit together on a bench again. Benches, cars, workbenches, touchlines and riverbanks are the furniture of men's friendship. Notice which ones are still in your life, and which have quietly gone.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's friendships were maintained as well by occasional face-to-face meetings as by regular shared activity. The evidence on how friendships form and fade, described in the chapter on shared activity, suggests that regular contact matters, but the best mix differs from person to person.

poseGallery.doCaption: Side by side, eyes on the view
poseGallery.annotation: For a man who finds personal talk hard, a table can feel like an interview. A bench, a car or a riverbank lowers the stakes.
A walk gives the eyes somewhere to go and the body a shared rhythm. Pauses feel like part of the walk, not like failures of the conversation.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Side by side, but turned away
poseGallery.annotation: Side by side is not the same as turned away. Bodies should still share a space, so that either person can look across when they want to.

poseGallery.doCaption: Turning to face for what matters
poseGallery.dontCaption: An apology made to the side of a head
poseGallery.annotation: Some things need the face. Turn toward someone for an apology or a serious announcement, and say that you are doing it on purpose.

poseGallery.doCaption: A phone call on a walk, eyes on the road ahead
poseGallery.dontCaption: A video call, both faces fixed on the screen
poseGallery.annotation: Many men find it easier to talk without a face to hold. A call while walking keeps the body busy and the gaze free.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Two men standing apart, glancing, with nothing to do
poseGallery.annotation: A shared task gives both people a reason to be there and somewhere to look, and talk often follows.

caseStudy:
Joe, forty-one, and Matt, forty-three, have been friends since school. For years they played five-a-side together on Thursdays, until the pitch closed and Matt's knee went. Since then they have met about twice a year, in a pub, across a table, catching up on news. When Joe's marriage ends, Matt hears about it from someone else.

Matt suggests a pint, and it goes badly. Joe gives a short, cheerful account of the separation, looks at his phone, and talks about football. Matt asks how he is really doing, and Joe says he is fine, holding Matt's gaze a little too steadily, and goes to the bar.

A month later Matt needs to collect a trailer from a town two hours away and asks Joe to come with him. Joe agrees, mainly because it sounds like a job rather than a conversation. For the first hour they talk about the route and the radio. Then, on a long straight stretch, Joe says, to the windscreen, that the worst part is the kids' bedrooms at his new flat, made up and empty on weekdays. His voice drops. Matt keeps his eyes on the road, says that sounds brutal, and waits. Joe talks for forty minutes, with long gaps.

At one point Joe turns his head and looks at Matt, as if checking. Matt glances across, nods once, and looks back at the road. Joe carries on. Matt does not try to fix anything. When they stop for petrol, they talk about the trailer.

On the way home Matt suggests they do something like it every month. They start walking a stretch of the coast path on the first Saturday of each month. Most of those walks are about nothing much. Some of them are about everything.
observe: Notice where your best conversations with male friends have happened, and which way you were facing at the time.
Notice, in a café or a pub, how pairs of people arrange themselves, without assuming why any particular pair chose its position.
Notice how often, in a face-to-face conversation, you or the other person look away while thinking.
Notice when someone beside you turns to face you, and what they say next.

drills.name: Map Your Conversations
steps: List five of the most meaningful conversations you have had with men in your life.
For each, write where you were and which way you were facing.
Note what you were doing with your hands and eyes at the time.
Look for a pattern: which settings made talk easier for you, and for the other person?
Write one sentence about what this tells you about how you prefer to talk.
variations: Do the same exercise for conversations with women in your life, and compare the settings.
Ask a close friend where he thinks your best conversations together have happened, and compare his answer with yours.

drills.name: The Invitation
steps: Choose a friend you have not seen properly for a while.
Write three invitations that involve doing something side by side rather than meeting to talk.
Choose the one that best suits him, not only you.
Send it this week, and make the activity the point.
variations: Invite someone you have lost touch with to help you with a small practical job rather than to meet for a drink.
Suggest a regular side-by-side activity, such as a monthly walk, rather than a one-off meeting.

drills.name: Read Without the Face
steps: On your next walk, drive or shared job with someone, notice changes in their voice, breath, hands and pace.
Each time you notice a change, note silently what was being talked about.
Resist the urge to turn and stare; glance briefly if they look across.
Afterwards, write down two changes and what you thought they meant.
If it is appropriate, check one of your readings later by asking a gentle question.
variations: Try reading someone on a phone call while you both walk, and note which channels you rely on.
Notice your own voice and breath when a conversation beside someone turns serious, and what you do with your hands.

drills.name: The Turn
steps: List three conversations you expect to have in the next few months that might need the face: an apology, bad news, a decision.
For each, decide where you will be and how you will turn to face the person.
Write the sentence you will use to mark the turn, such as “I want to look at you while I say this.”
Practise saying it aloud until it sounds like you.
variations: Practise the turn with someone close to you in a low-stakes moment, such as thanking them for something.
Ask someone close to you which conversations they would rather have face to face, and note their answers.

quiz.q: A friend says that men's friendships are shallower than women's, because men just do things together. What does the research suggest?
options: He is right: men disclose almost nothing to friends at any age
Men's friendships are deeper, because shared activity outlasts talk
Differences are real but modest, and many men share a great deal
There are no differences of any kind between men's and women's friendships
quiz.explain: Wright's side-by-side description and Hall's meta-analysis point to modest average differences in what men and women expect from friends, with heavy overlap. Side by side describes how many men prefer to be close, not a limit on closeness.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter suggest that side-by-side conversation can make hard things easier to say?
options: It removes the work of managing and watching faces while finding words
It prevents the listener from ever hearing what the speaker means
It guarantees that the other person cannot see how you feel inside
It forces both people to talk faster, so there is less time for fear
quiz.explain: Holding eye contact while thinking is effortful, and people look away when questions get harder. Side by side lowers that load and makes pauses feel natural rather than awkward.

quiz.q: What did Boothby, Clark and Bargh find when two people tasted the same chocolate at the same time?
options: The shared experience was rated more intensely, whether pleasant or not
People enjoyed the chocolate less whenever anyone else was in the room
Talking about the taste was needed before any shared effect appeared
Only close friends showed any change in how the chocolate was rated
quiz.explain: Sharing an experience without talking amplified it: pleasant chocolate seemed more pleasant and bitter chocolate more bitter. Attending to the same thing together seems to build something of its own.

quiz.q: You are driving with a friend who has gone quiet. His voice drops as he starts to talk about his father's illness. What fits this chapter best?
options: Pull over at once so you can look him in the eye while he talks
Keep your eyes on the road, say a short supportive word, and wait
Change the subject to something lighter so he does not get upset
Turn and watch his face closely so you can read how he feels
quiz.explain: A drive works because neither person has to manage their face. Stay with him through your voice and your patience, and save anything more demanding for when the car has stopped.

quiz.q: Which situation most calls for turning to face someone rather than staying side by side?
options: Watching a match together while talking about the team's season
Walking a familiar route while chatting about the week's news
Working together on an engine while one of you talks about work
Apologising to a friend for something you did that hurt him
quiz.explain: An apology asks the other person to see you, and to see that you are seeing them. Side by side suits easing into talk, not every kind of talk.

quiz.q: A man notices that he and his oldest friend have gone from weekly football to two pub meetings a year. What does this chapter suggest he try first?
options: Book a long face-to-face dinner to discuss why they drifted apart
Wait for his friend to make contact, since he moved away first
Invite his friend to do something regular together, side by side
Accept that friendships between men naturally end in middle age
quiz.explain: Side-by-side friendships often fade when the shared activity ends. Restoring a regular activity usually does more than scheduling a talk about the friendship.

quiz.q: What did Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz find about walking?
options: Most people came up with more creative ideas walking than sitting
Walking made almost everyone less creative, because attention was split between two tasks
Walking improved creativity only for professional athletes who walked every single day
Walking had no effect on thinking, though people said they enjoyed it rather more
quiz.explain: Most participants generated more creative ideas while walking than while sitting. A walk side by side can help a problem that went round in circles at a desk open up.

quiz.q: You prefer to talk on walks, but your partner says she feels avoided when you suggest a walk every time she raises something serious. What fits this chapter best?
options: Keep suggesting walks, since side by side is always the better way to talk
Ask how she prefers to talk, and turn to face her for the things that matter
Stop talking about serious things altogether, since you clearly disagree on how
Tell her that research proves walking conversations are more honest than any other kind
quiz.explain: Side by side is useful, not universal. Some people feel heard only when they are looked at, and some conversations ask for the face. Ask, and be ready to turn.

quiz.q: Someone says that Men's Sheds have been proven to cure loneliness in older men. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since large trials have shown that every man who joins is cured
The idea is promising, but the evidence is mixed and mostly from small studies
It is wrong, since the research shows that Men's Sheds make loneliness worse
It is right, but only for men who were tradesmen during their working lives
quiz.explain: A review by Wilson and Cordier found reports of benefits, but most studies were small. Men's Sheds are a promising setting for side-by-side connection, not a proven cure.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific friendship with a man that matters to you. Where have your best conversations with him happened, and which way were you facing? Is there something that has gone unsaid between you, or something you suspect he is carrying? Describe a side-by-side setting where you could spend time with him in the next month, what you would do, and whether there is anything that would need you to turn and face him instead.
reflection.guidance: Be concrete about the setting: a particular walk, a drive, a job, a match. If you cannot think of a setting you still share, that is worth noticing in itself, and the first step may be to create one. If something needs saying face to face, write the first sentence you would use.

failureMode: The first failure is to read side by side as proof that men's friendships are shallow, rather than as a common way of being close. The second is to stare: to turn and watch a man who is trying to talk to the windscreen, putting back the spotlight that the arrangement removed. The third is to use side by side to avoid, spending years beside a friend at matches without either of you ever saying that something is wrong. The fourth is to stay beside someone when the moment needs the face, such as an apology or bad news, or to push someone who prefers face to face into your preferred arrangement. And the fifth is to let the settings for side-by-side friendship disappear, and then wonder why the friendship did.

furtherStudy.work: Men's friendships, women's friendships and the alleged inferiority of the latter
furtherStudy.author: Paul H. Wright
furtherStudy.note: Sex Roles 8(1), 1982. The paper that introduced side-by-side and face-to-face friendship, and argued against reading one as inferior.

furtherStudy.work: Sex differences in friendship expectations: A meta-analysis
furtherStudy.author: Jeffrey A. Hall
furtherStudy.note: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships 28(6), 2011. How large, and how small, the differences really are.

furtherStudy.author: Erica J. Boothby, Margaret S. Clark and John A. Bargh
furtherStudy.note: Psychological Science 25(12), 2014. Why attending to the same thing together changes the experience.

furtherStudy.author: Geoffrey L. Greif
furtherStudy.note: Oxford University Press, 2009. Interviews with hundreds of men about how their friendships form, last and end.

moreCases.title: The drive to the station
moreCases.scene:
Paul, forty-eight, has been trying for weeks to find out what is bothering his son, Callum, seventeen. Callum has gone quiet since the autumn, spends most evenings in his room, and gives one-word answers at dinner. Twice Paul has sat him down at the kitchen table, looked him in the eye and asked what is wrong. Both times Callum has said nothing is, stared at the table, and gone back upstairs as soon as he could. Paul's wife thinks he is pushing too hard. Paul thinks he is not pushing hard enough.

On a dark Tuesday morning in January, Callum misses the bus to college, and Paul drives him to the station, twenty minutes away. For the first ten minutes they say nothing. The radio is on. Then, at a red light, without looking at his father, Callum says that he is not sure he wants to go to university after all, and that he does not know how to tell his mum, because she has been talking about it since he was eleven.

Paul's first instinct is to pull over, turn round and talk about it properly.

Paul remembers that his own father never asked him anything at the table either, and that the only real conversation they ever had was in a car, on the way to Paul's first job interview. He had forgotten that until now.

Paul also notices that Callum chose the moment himself: a red light, with something to look at, the radio on, and fifteen minutes left before the station. Nothing Paul had arranged had worked. The one setting he had not arranged did.
moreCases.misread:
Paul read the kitchen table as the right place for a serious conversation, because that is where serious conversations happen in films and in his own childhood. He read Callum's silence there as stubbornness, and his own urge to turn and face him in the car as taking the matter seriously.

And because both kitchen conversations had failed, Paul had started to believe that Callum simply did not want to talk to him, which made the urge to seize the moment in the car all the stronger.

His wife's view, that he was pushing, was right about the table and wrong about the need. Callum wanted to talk. He needed a different shape of conversation.
moreCases.betterRead:
Face to face, across a table, a teenager has nowhere to look but at the person questioning him, and every hesitation is watched. In the car, with the road to look at, the radio filling the silence and a fixed time before arrival, the load drops, and Callum said in ten minutes what he had not been able to say in weeks. Paul's better reading was to keep the arrangement that had made it possible. He did not pull over. He kept his eyes on the road, turned the radio down a little, and said, "Thanks for telling me. That sounds like a lot to carry." He asked what Callum was thinking of doing instead, and listened. At the station he said they could talk more on the drive home if Callum wanted, and offered to pick him up. Callum said yes. Over three evening drives that week, they worked out how to tell his mother together.

Paul also stopped holding serious conversations at the kitchen table, and started offering lifts.

moreCases.title: The widower at the workbench
moreCases.scene:
Arthur, seventy-two, was an electrician for forty years. Since his wife died two years ago, he has spent most days alone in his bungalow. His daughter worries about him. She has tried to get him to join a bereavement group, which he went to once and hated. "Sitting in a circle talking about feelings," he told her. "Not for me."

A neighbour mentions a Men's Shed that has opened in the old scout hut: a workshop where retired men make and mend things together. Arthur goes, reluctantly, on a Thursday morning. He spends the first hour standing near the door. Then someone asks whether anyone knows how to rewire an old lamp. Arthur does.

By the end of the morning he is at a workbench with two other men, his back to the room, his hands busy, talking about lamps, then about the football, then, briefly and without looking up, about his wife.

Arthur's daughter has also noticed that he answers the phone more cheerfully on Thursday evenings, and that he has started mentioning names she does not know: Bill, Gordon, a man called Taff who apparently cannot hammer a nail straight.

Arthur's daughter rang him that evening and asked how it had gone. He said it was all right, and then talked for twenty minutes about a lamp, a man called Gordon and the state of the shed's electrics, which he intends to fix.
moreCases.misread:
Arthur's daughter read the bereavement group as the natural route to support, because it offered talk. Arthur read talk about feelings, in a circle, face to face, as something not for men like him, and so he had concluded that support was not for him either.

The group itself was not wrong. It was simply arranged in a way that put Arthur's face on show at the moment he least wanted to be seen.

And Arthur's own reading, that support was not for men like him, would have kept him at home if the only kind on offer had been a circle of chairs.
moreCases.betterRead:
For many men, closeness grows out of doing something alongside others, as Paul Wright described. A circle of chairs puts every face on show; a workbench puts every pair of hands to work and every face towards the job. Arthur did not talk about his wife because anyone asked him to. He talked about her because he was beside two men with something to do and no one watching his face. Men's Sheds and similar groups are a promising idea, and a review by Wilson and Cordier found reports of benefits to wellbeing and social connection, though the evidence is mixed and mostly from small studies. They are not a cure for grief or loneliness. But for men like Arthur they can offer a setting where the side-by-side principle does its work. His daughter's better approach, once she saw it, was to stop pushing the group and start asking about the lamps. He goes every Thursday now, and on Tuesdays too.

She also learned to ask about the lamps first and the feelings second, and found that the feelings came along by themselves.

moreCases.title: The wife who wanted to be faced
moreCases.scene:
Rich and Hana have been married for eight years. Rich has read about side-by-side conversation and has become a convert. When he wants to talk about something important, he suggests a walk. When Hana wants to talk, he suggests they go for a drive. On the walks he talks easily, and he is proud of how much more open he has become.

Hana is not happy. She tells her sister that whenever she raises anything serious, Rich steers them out of the house, and that she has started to feel he does not want to look at her. Last week, when she tried to tell him how lonely she had felt since the baby was born, he suggested a walk round the park. She said no, she wanted to sit down and look at him. He looked confused, and a bit hurt.

When Hana's sister asks whether she has told Rich this, Hana says she should not have to.

Rich, for his part, has been trying hard. He has read that men open up more on walks, and he has been proud of finally learning to talk. It has not occurred to him that what works for him might not work for her.

Rich grew up in a house where the only real conversations happened in the car or on the allotment, and he has always found eye contact during hard talk almost unbearable. Hana grew up in a family that sat round the kitchen table every night and talked about everything.
moreCases.misread:
Rich read side by side as the best way to talk for everyone, because it worked so well for him. Hana read his suggestions of walks and drives as a way of avoiding her face, and his confusion as proof that he did not understand.

Hana's view that she should not have to tell him was understandable, and it left Rich guessing, which is how misreadings in long relationships tend to persist.

Each of them was reading the other through their own childhood, which is one of the commonest sources of misreading in long relationships.
moreCases.betterRead: Side by side is a useful arrangement, not a rule. This chapter's block on when to turn and face makes the point that some people prefer face to face, and should not be pushed beside you because it is easier for you. Hall's review found that women, on average, expected more intimacy and self-disclosure from friends, and for many people being looked at while they speak is part of feeling heard. Some conversations, such as telling a partner you have been lonely, ask to be seen. The better approach was for both of them to say what they needed. When Hana did tell him, Rich was shocked and apologetic. They agreed that either of them could ask for a walk or a sit-down, and that the other would say yes. That evening, they sat on the sofa facing each other, and Rich kept his eyes on her face while she talked, which he found hard and which she said made all the difference.

moreCases.title: Thirty years of fishing, and one thing unsaid
moreCases.scene:
Keith and Barry, both sixty-one, have fished together on the same river every second Saturday for thirty years. They talk about the weather, the river, the football and their grandchildren. They are, by any measure, close friends. In the spring, Barry is diagnosed with prostate cancer. He tells his wife and his doctor. He does not tell Keith.

For three months they keep fishing. Keith notices that Barry is thinner, that he has missed two Saturdays for "appointments", and that he sits more and casts less. Keith wonders, but does not ask. They have never asked each other anything like that.

Then Barry's wife mentions the diagnosis to Keith's wife, assuming he already knew. Keith is hurt, and then ashamed. He realises that in thirty years beside each other, they have never said a single thing that mattered.

Keith also remembers that when his own father was dying, nobody in the family said so aloud until the last week. He had sworn he would be different, and then had been exactly the same.

Barry's wife has been urging him to tell Keith for weeks. Barry keeps saying that he will, next Saturday, and every Saturday the river is calm and the light is good, and the moment never seems right. He tells his wife afterwards that it would have felt like dropping a stone into the water.
moreCases.misread:
Both men read their side-by-side friendship as a place where some things are not said, and read the silence about Barry's health as respect. Keith read his own unasked questions as tact.

Barry, for his part, read Keith's silence as a sign that he did not want to know, when Keith had simply not known how to ask.

Keith also read Barry's thinner frame and missed Saturdays with the same tact he had always used, which kept the friendship comfortable and left Barry alone with the hardest thing in his life. The arrangement that made talking easy had become the reason neither of them did.

Neither man was unkind. Each was waiting for the other, and the river made waiting easy.
moreCases.betterRead: Side by side lowers the cost of saying hard things; it does not say them for you. The failure this chapter warns about is using the arrangement to avoid rather than to approach: spending years beside a friend without either of you ever saying what matters. The setting Keith and Barry shared was ideal for the conversation. What was missing was one of them starting it. Keith's better approach, the next Saturday, was to use the river. With both of them looking at the water, he said, "I heard about the diagnosis, mate. I wish you'd told me. How are you doing with it?" Barry said nothing for a while, then that he had not wanted to spoil the fishing. Keith said that nothing would spoil the fishing, and that he would drive him to his appointments if he wanted. They talked for an hour without once looking at each other. On the drive home, at Barry's door, Keith turned in his seat and looked at him, and said, "I mean it. Anything you need." Barry nodded and held his eyes, and got out of the car.

workedReading.title: Reading a friend on a long drive
workedReading.scene:
Sam is driving his friend Dev to Dev's father's eightieth birthday, three hours each way. Dev's father has dementia, and Dev has said little about it. For the first hour they talk about work and football. Then, as they pass the turning for the town where Dev grew up, Dev goes quiet. Sam glances across. Dev is looking out of the side window, his jaw set, his hands pressed flat on his thighs.

Sam knows Dev well. They have been friends for twenty years, and he has seen Dev quiet like this only twice before: after his divorce, and when his mother was ill.

Dev has visited his father only twice since the diagnosis, and both times he came home and did not speak for the rest of the day. He asked Sam to drive this time, he said, because he did not trust himself to drive back. Sam took that as a sign that this journey matters more than either of them has said.

steps.label: Keep the arrangement
steps.text:
Sam's first impulse is to turn down the radio and ask what is wrong. He holds back. The car is working: Dev can look out of the window, nobody is watching his face, and there are two hours left. Sam keeps his eyes on the road and his voice light, and decides to let Dev set the pace.

He also keeps driving at the same steady speed, and does not change lanes or overtake for a while. A smooth, predictable drive keeps the setting calm.

He also reminds himself that Dev chose to go quiet at exactly the place where his childhood begins. The setting is doing some of the work, and it does not need any help from him.

steps.label: Glance, do not stare
steps.text:
He checks on Dev only in brief glances, the way any driver glances at a passenger. He sees the jaw, the flat hands, the eyes on the window. He does not turn his head to look properly, because that would put back the spotlight that the car removed.

He also notes that Dev's body is turned slightly away, towards the window. That is not rejection. It is a man giving himself a little more privacy inside a small space.

He also keeps his own body relaxed: one hand on the wheel, shoulders down, no sudden movements. A tense driver makes a tense passenger.

steps.label: Listen to the voice
steps.text:
When Dev eventually speaks, saying that they used to drive this road every summer to his gran's, Sam listens to his voice more than his words. It is lower and slower than it was an hour ago, with a pause before "gran's", and the last words trail off. The voice says more than the sentence: this is close to something that hurts.

He also answers in a voice that matches Dev's: lower and slower. A bright, chatty reply would have told Dev that the moment had not been noticed.

He also notes what Dev does not say. He talks about his gran and the summers, not about his father. The avoidance is part of the message: the hardest thing is still being approached from the side.

steps.label: Listen to the breath and hands
steps.text:
Sam notices a long breath out through Dev's nose, and that one of Dev's hands has moved to rub the back of his neck, a pacifier described in Part I. Dev is not just remembering a road. He is bracing for the visit, and soothing himself while he does it.

He also notices that Dev's hand stays on his neck while he talks about his gran, and moves away when he changes the subject. The pacifier marks the topic that hurts.

He also notices that he wants to fix it: to say that his father will probably recognise him, that it will be fine. He lets the urge pass, because he does not know that it is true, and Dev would know he did not.

steps.label: Let the silence work
steps.text:
Sam says, "Good summers?" and nothing more. Dev says yes, and then nothing for nearly a mile. Sam does not fill the gap. In a car, silence is easy to bear, because the road keeps moving. When Dev speaks again, it is to say that his dad did not know who he was on the phone last week, and that he is dreading walking into the room.

He also turns the radio off at some point during the silence, quietly, without comment. The gesture tells Dev that the space is his, without a single word.

When Dev does speak, Sam answers with a question about the dread, not about the dementia. "What's the worst bit?" lets Dev choose what to say next.

steps.label: Turn for what matters
steps.text:
Sam listens, says that sounds really hard, and asks what he can do. At the service station, an hour later, they stop for coffee. As they stand by the car, Sam turns and faces Dev, and says, "I'll come in with you, if you want. Or I'll wait in the car. Your call." He wants Dev to see him say it.

He chooses the service station deliberately. Standing by the car, with a coffee each, is a natural place to turn and face someone, and then to go back to driving.

He also keeps the turn short. Two sentences, face to face, and then back to the car. Turning for what matters does not mean turning the whole journey into a heart-to-heart.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Dev asks him to come in. At the party, Sam stays beside him, which is where Dev seems to want him. On the drive home, Dev talks for most of the three hours, about his father, his childhood and his fears, all of it to the windscreen. When Sam drops him off, Dev says that it was the best day he has had in months, which surprises them both.

Sam also texts Dev the next day, briefly, to ask how he is, and suggests another drive in a month, to visit his father again if Dev wants company.

Sam also notes, for himself, how much he learned without seeing Dev's face for most of the day: the voice, the breath, the hand on the neck, the place on the road where he went quiet. He had read his friend more clearly from the side than he ever had across a table.

moreFailures.title: Treating side by side as shallow
moreFailures.body:
It is common to hear that men's friendships are thinner than women's, because men just do things together while women really talk. The research is more nuanced. Hall's review of thirty-seven studies found real but modest differences in what men and women expect from friends, with a great deal of overlap, and plenty of evidence that men value closeness and support as much as women do. Side by side is a different route to closeness, not a lack of it. Judging men's friendships by a face-to-face standard misses the conversations that happen in cars, on walks and at workbenches, and it can make men feel that their way of being close does not count.

It also helps to notice how men themselves talk about it. Many describe a friend as someone they could ring at three in the morning, even if they have never talked about feelings with him. That is a kind of closeness, not a lack of it.

It also helps to notice the language used to describe men's friendships: "just mates", "only football", "not really close". These can hide how much those friendships matter, sometimes from the men themselves.

And it helps to remember that many women value side-by-side time too: walks with friends, cooking together, a shared project. The pattern is about what makes talk easier, not about who is allowed to have it.

moreFailures.title: Staring at the man beside you
moreFailures.body:
The whole point of side by side is that nobody has to hold anyone's gaze. When a man starts to talk to the windscreen, the instinct of a caring listener is to turn and watch him properly, to show that they are paying attention. That puts back exactly the pressure the arrangement removed, and many men will stop talking. Glance as a passenger or a walking companion would, briefly and naturally. Let your voice show that you are listening: a murmur, a short question, an unhurried silence. Read through the channels the chapter describes, voice, breath and hands, rather than through his face.

It also helps to resist commenting on the conversation itself. Saying "It's great that we're finally talking like this" can make a man self-conscious and end it. Let it be ordinary.

Partners and parents often make this mistake out of love. When a man finally starts talking, they want to show that they are listening with their whole body. Showing it with your voice, and keeping your eyes on the road, works better.

moreFailures.title: Using side by side to avoid
moreFailures.body:
Shared activity can become a place to hide. Years of matches, fishing trips or rounds of golf can go by without either friend ever saying that one of them is ill, divorcing, grieving or struggling. The arrangement makes hard things easier to say, but someone still has to say them. If you have a side-by-side friendship and something is going on, use the setting: say the thing while you both look at the river. If your friend seems to be carrying something, ask, once, plainly, as the chapter on the I'm Fine mask describes, and let the activity carry the silence afterwards.

A useful habit is to make one honest remark on every outing: how you really are, one sentence. It keeps the door open without turning the activity into an interview.

If you notice that years have passed without any real conversation, the next outing is a good time to change it. One plain sentence, said while you both look at the same thing, is enough to start.

It also helps to know that men often regret, later, what was never said in these friendships, especially after a friend has died. Saying it now, however awkwardly, is almost always the better choice.

moreFailures.title: Assuming everyone wants it
moreFailures.body:
Side by side works well for many men, and for many women too, but not for everyone and not for every conversation. Some people feel heard only when they are looked at. Some find walks or drives a way of being avoided. Some conversations, such as apologies, declarations, bad news and decisions that will change a relationship, ask for the face. Do not make side by side your only mode, and do not push it on people because it suits you. Ask how the other person likes to talk, and be ready to turn and face them when it matters.

It also helps to watch the other person's response when you suggest side by side. If they hesitate, look disappointed or say "can we just sit?", take it as information about what they need.

It also helps to switch modes for the end of a conversation. Even a walk that has gone well can end with a moment face to face, a look and a word, so that the other person knows they were seen as well as heard.

questions.q: Is it true that men only bond through activities?
questions.a:
No. Wright's phrase, side by side versus face to face, describes a tendency, not a rule. Hall's meta-analysis found that, on average, women expected more self-disclosure and intimacy from friends and men placed more weight on shared activity, but the differences were modest and the overlap large. Many men have deep face-to-face friendships, and many women bond through shared activity. Activity is often the setting that makes men's closeness possible, and it is easy to underestimate how much is being shared in it. The useful question is not which is better, but which works for this person and this conversation.

It also helps to remember that friendships change over a lifetime. Men who bonded through sport in their twenties may find, in their fifties, that they want and can manage more direct talk. The route can change as the friendship does.

It also helps to notice that men often talk more about their friendships than people expect, when asked about the activities rather than the feelings. "Who do you go fishing with?" can open a conversation that "Who are you close to?" would close.

It also helps to notice that the setting is not the friendship. Two men who meet only at football can be very close, and two men who talk for hours can be strangers to each other. What matters is what passes between them.

questions.q: Why do children talk so much in the car?
questions.a:
For the same reasons adults do. In a car, nobody has to make eye contact, there is something to look at, the journey has a natural end, and silence is easy to bear because the road keeps moving. Children and teenagers often raise the things they find hardest to say on the school run, at bedtime with the light off, or while doing something with a parent, such as cooking or walking the dog. Many parents find that a fixed weekly drive, a walk or a shared task does more for conversation than any amount of sitting down at the kitchen table to talk.

It also helps to keep the drive or walk going after the hard thing is said. Stopping the car or turning round to face them can make it feel like a confession; carrying on lets it be part of an ordinary journey.

It also explains why bedtime, with the light off, is such a common time for children to say what is on their minds. In the dark, nobody can see anyone's face.

questions.q: What if we do not share a hobby?
questions.a:
You do not need one. Side by side can be built from almost anything that gives two people something to look at and do: a walk, an errand, a drive to the tip, cooking a meal, watching a match, washing the car, a job on the house, volunteering together. The activity does not need to be important, only shared. Many friendships that have faded can be restarted by inviting someone to help with a small task, such as moving a sofa or fixing a fence, because it gives both of you a reason to be there that is not about talking.

It also helps to make it regular. A standing arrangement, the same walk on the first Sunday of every month, removes the need to arrange each meeting and gives the friendship a rhythm.

It also helps to suggest the activity rather than the conversation. "Fancy a walk on Sunday?" is easy to say yes to. "Can we have a talk?" is not.

Shared tasks also have an end, which helps. When the sofa is moved or the fence is fixed, there is a natural moment to stop, and nobody has to find a way to leave a conversation.

questions.q: Does this work on the phone?
questions.a:
In part. A phone call removes the face, which is why many men find calls easier than video, and why some find it easier still to talk while walking with a phone, so that their eyes and bodies are occupied. But a call also removes the shared activity and the shared view, and long silences feel heavier on the phone than in a car. For hard conversations at a distance, a call is usually better than a video call or a message, and a walking call can be better still. For the most important things, being in the same place, side by side or face to face, is still best.

It also helps to agree in advance that silences are fine. On a walking call, saying "I'm just walking, no rush" makes it easier for the other person to take their time.

It also helps to keep the camera off on video calls when the subject is hard, if both people are comfortable with that. Many people find it easier to talk when they are not looking at their own face on the screen.

For some men, messages work in a similar way. A conversation that unfolds over days by text, with no faces and no pressure to reply at once, can carry things that would be hard to say on a call.

questions.q: How can I read someone when I cannot see their face?
questions.a:
Through the other channels this book has taught. Listen to the voice: pace, pitch, volume, pauses and where the voice drops. Listen to the breath: sighs, held breaths, the catch before a hard word. Watch the hands and the body with the edge of your attention: a hand rubbing the neck, fingers tapping, a body turning slightly towards or away. Notice silence, and what it follows. And notice the words themselves, which often matter more than anything else when someone is speaking to the windscreen. You will see less than face to face, and you will often hear more.

It also helps to check your reading afterwards, gently, if it matters. "You went quiet when we passed your old school. All right?" turns a guess into a question.

It also helps to accept that you will miss some things. Side by side trades some information for some ease, and for many conversations that is a good trade.

questions.q: Are Men's Sheds and similar groups worth it?
questions.a:
For some men, they may be. Men's Sheds offer a workshop where men make and mend things together, and many men who would never join a support group find their way there. A review by Wilson and Cordier found reports of benefits to wellbeing and social connection, but most studies were small and the evidence is mixed, so they should be seen as promising rather than proven. Similar ideas include walking groups, community gardens, volunteering and sports clubs for older men. If someone you know is isolated and dislikes the idea of talking groups, a place where men do things side by side may be an easier door to walk through.

It also helps to go with them the first time. Many men find it far easier to walk into a new group alongside a friend than on their own.

It may also help to look for groups where the activity is genuinely the point, rather than a pretext. Men are often quick to spot a support group dressed up as something else, and slow to trust it.

And if the person resists, keep the door open. A man who says no to a Men's Shed this month may say yes to a walk with a neighbour next month, or to the shed in a year.

watch.title: The Trip to Spain: Official Trailer
watch.notice: Two men talk their way across Spain, side by side in a car and across restaurant tables. Notice how much of their friendship happens while both of them are looking ahead.

reviewPrompt: This week, invite one friend to do something side by side with you, and notice what gets said that would not have been said across a table.
